es.summary: Pérdida involuntaria de orina que ocurre después de una necesidad súbita de vaciar la vejiga, típica de la vejiga hiperactiva.
key_points: Se asocia a contracciones involuntarias del detrusor.
Frecuente en adultos mayores y pacientes con infecciones urinarias o trastornos neurológicos.
Diagnóstico basado en historia, diario miccional y pruebas de flujo/volumen residual.
Tratamiento de primera línea: entrenamiento vesical y anticolinérgicos.

pathophysiology: Desinhibición del reflejo de micción provoca contracciones espontáneas del detrusor.
Sensibilidad aumentada de los receptores de estiramiento vesical.
Falta de coordinación entre detrusor y esfínter externo durante la urgencia.
risk_factors: Enfermedades neurológicas (ES, esclerosis múltiple, lesión medular).
Consumo excesivo de cafeína o alcohol.
signs_symptoms: Necesidad repentina e intensa de orinar.
Pérdida de pequeñas cantidades de orina antes de llegar al baño.
No hay retención significativa ni goteo constante.
diagnostics: Historia clínica y diario miccional (volumen, frecuencia, desencadenantes).
Análisis de orina: descartar ITU (leucocitos, nitritos).
Ecografía renal y vesical: volumen residual postmiccional <100 mL.
Uroflujometría: patrón de flujo normal o ligeramente alterado.
treatment: Ejercicios de Kegel para fortalecer el suelo pélvico.
complications: Irritación y dermatitis perineal por humedad.
Aislamiento social y disminución de la calidad de vida.
nursing_care: Evaluar frecuencia, volumen y desencadenantes mediante diario miccional.
Inspeccionar piel perineal en cada turno; registrar enrojecimiento o maceración.
Mantener higiene perineal con agua tibia y secado suave después de cada episodio.
Colocar al paciente en posición semisentada para facilitar el vaciado completo.
Monitorear signos de ITU: fiebre, dolor suprapúbico, cambios en orina.
patient_teaching: Practicar entrenamiento vesical: ir al baño cada 2‑3 h, incluso sin urgencia.
Realizar ejercicios de Kegel 3 series de 10 repeticiones, tres veces al día.
Limitar ingesta de cafeína a <200 mg/día y evitar alcohol en exceso.
Mantener hidratación adecuada (≈30 mL/kg/día) y registrar ingesta de líquidos.
Usar ropa interior absorbente y cambiarla frecuentemente para proteger la piel.

outcomes: Infección del tracto urinario: ausencia de fiebre y leucocituria en 48 h.
Integridad cutánea perineal: piel sin enrojecimiento ni maceración en 72 h.

interventions.action: Realizar higiene perineal con agua tibia y secado suave después de cada episodio de incontinencia.
interventions.rationale: Reduce la carga bacteriana y previene la colonización que puede causar ITU.

interventions.action: Registrar y monitorear el diario miccional para identificar patrones de urgencia.
interventions.rationale: Permite anticipar episodios y programar vaciado, disminuyendo la exposición prolongada a la humedad.

interventions.action: Aplicar barrera cutánea (crema protectora) en zona perineal según necesidad.
interventions.rationale: Protege la piel de la irritación y crea una barrera contra microorganismos.

interventions.action: Educar al paciente sobre consumo adecuado de líquidos y evitar irritantes.
interventions.rationale: Mantener flujo urinario adecuado reduce estasis y riesgo de infección.

interventions.action: Notificar al médico cualquier signo de ITU (fiebre, disuria, leucocituria).
interventions.rationale: Intervención temprana evita complicaciones sistémicas.

related_to: exposición prolongada a humedad por incontinencia
outcomes: Integridad cutánea: piel perineal sin lesiones visibles en 72 h.
Confort del paciente: reporte de ausencia de dolor o ardor perineal en 48 h.

interventions.action: Inspeccionar la zona perineal en cada turno y documentar hallazgos.
interventions.rationale: Detección temprana permite intervención oportuna para prevenir ulceración.

interventions.action: Cambiar ropa interior absorbente cada 2‑3 h o cuando esté húmeda.
interventions.rationale: Reduce la exposición a la humedad que causa maceración cutánea.

interventions.action: Aplicar crema hidratante o barrera según protocolo de la unidad.
interventions.rationale: Mantiene la integridad de la epidermis y previene irritación.

interventions.action: Enseñar al paciente técnicas de secado suave (toque ligero, no frotar).
interventions.rationale: Evita daño mecánico a la piel ya comprometida.

interventions.action: Evaluar necesidad de dispositivos de absorción alternativos (pañales de adulto con capa transpirable).
interventions.rationale: Mejora la ventilación cutánea y disminuye riesgo de dermatitis.

en.summary: Unintentional loss of urine that occurs after a sudden need to empty the bladder, typical of overactive bladder.
key_points: Common in older adults and patients with urinary tract infections or neurological disorders.
Diagnosis based on history, bladder diary, and flow/ residual volume tests.
First‑line treatment: bladder training and anticholinergics.

pathophysiology: Disinhibition of the micturition reflex causes spontaneous detrusor contractions.
Increased sensitivity of bladder stretch receptors.
Lack of coordination between detrusor and external sphincter during urgency.
risk_factors: Neurological diseases (MS, multiple sclerosis, spinal cord injury).
signs_symptoms: Sudden and intense need to urinate.
Loss of small amounts of urine before reaching the bathroom.
No significant retention or constant dribbling.
diagnostics: Medical history and bladder diary (volume, frequency, triggers).
Renal and bladder ultrasound: post‑void residual <100 mL.
Uroflowmetry: normal or slightly altered flow pattern.
treatment: Kegel exercises to strengthen pelvic floor.
Bladder training with scheduled voiding times.
complications: Perineal irritation and dermatitis from moisture.
Social isolation and decreased quality of life.
Falls from rushing to the bathroom.
nursing_care: Assess frequency, volume, and triggers using a bladder diary.
Inspect perineal skin each shift; document redness or maceration.
Maintain perineal hygiene with warm water and gentle drying after each episode.
Position patient semi‑upright to facilitate complete emptying.
Monitor UTI signs: fever, suprapubic pain, changes in urine.
patient_teaching: Practice bladder training: go to the bathroom every 2‑3 h, even without urgency.
Perform Kegel exercises 3 sets of 10 repetitions, three times daily.
Limit caffeine intake to <200 mg/day and avoid excessive alcohol.
Maintain adequate hydration (≈30 mL/kg/day) and record fluid intake.
Use absorbent underwear and change frequently to protect the skin.

outcomes: Urinary tract infection: absence of fever and leukocyturia within 48 h.
Perineal skin integrity: skin without redness or maceration within 72 h.

interventions.action: Perform perineal hygiene with warm water and gentle drying after each incontinence episode.
interventions.rationale: Reduces bacterial load and prevents colonization that can cause UTI.

interventions.action: Record and monitor the bladder diary to identify urgency patterns.
interventions.rationale: Allows anticipation of episodes and scheduled voiding, decreasing prolonged moisture exposure.

interventions.action: Apply barrier cream to the perineal area as needed.
interventions.rationale: Protects skin from irritation and creates a barrier against microorganisms.

interventions.action: Educate the patient on adequate fluid intake and avoidance of irritants.
interventions.rationale: Maintaining adequate urine flow reduces stasis and infection risk.

interventions.action: Notify the physician of any UTI signs (fever, dysuria, leukocyturia).
interventions.rationale: Early intervention prevents systemic complications.

outcomes: Skin integrity: perineal skin without visible lesions within 72 h.
Patient comfort: report of no perineal pain or burning within 48 h.

interventions.action: Inspect the perineal area each shift and document findings.
interventions.rationale: Early detection allows timely intervention to prevent ulceration.

interventions.action: Change absorbent underwear every 2‑3 h or when wet.
interventions.rationale: Reduces moisture exposure that causes skin maceration.

interventions.action: Apply moisturizing or barrier cream per unit protocol.
interventions.rationale: Maintains epidermal integrity and prevents irritation.

interventions.action: Teach the patient gentle drying techniques (light touch, no rubbing).
interventions.rationale: Avoids mechanical damage to compromised skin.

interventions.action: Assess need for alternative absorbent devices (adult diapers with breathable layer).
interventions.rationale: Improves skin ventilation and reduces dermatitis risk.

sources.name: Fundamentals of Nursing: The Nurse’s Role in Urinary Elimination
Clinical Nursing Skills: Nursing Management of Elimination

key_points.2.quote: Your health care provider may use many tools to make a diagnosis: A medical history, which includes asking about your symptoms.

sections.risk_factors.1.quote: It can sometimes be a sign of a urinary tract infection (UTI) .

sections.risk_factors.2.quote: It can also happen in some neurological conditions , such as multiple sclerosis and spinal cord injuries .

sections.risk_factors.3.quote: In adults, the causes include some medicines, caffeine , and alcohol .

sections.signs_symptoms.0.quote: Urge, or urgency, incontinence happens when you have a strong urge (need) to urinate, and some urine leaks out before you can make it to the toilet.

sections.diagnostics.0.quote: The assessment process encompasses a detailed medical history, including the onset, frequency, and severity of incontinence episodes, as well as any potential triggers or exacerbating factors.

sections.diagnostics.1.quote: Nitrites None Presence may indicate bacterial infection, particularly urinary tract infection (UTI).

sections.treatment.0.quote: Strong pelvic floor muscles hold in urine better than weak muscles. The strengthening exercises are called Kegel exercises.

sections.treatment.1.quote: Timed voiding helps to control urge and overflow incontinence by training the brain to be less sensitive to the sensation of the bladder walls expanding as they fill (National Institute of Aging, 2022).

sections.complications.0.quote: Moisture-related dermatitis, often referred to as moisture-associated skin damage, is a skin condition characterized by inflammation and irritation resulting from prolonged exposure to moisture.

sections.complications.2.quote: Urinary incontinence is associated with a decreased quality of life and decreased interpersonal interaction due to embarrassment, frustration, depression, and loss of self-esteem.

sections.nursing_care.0.quote: The voiding diary should include the following: when and how much the patient urinates urinary leakage and what the patient was doing when it happened (e.g., running, biking, laughing) sudden urges to urinate how often the

sections.nursing_care.4.quote: Signs and symptoms of a CAUTI to urgently report to the healthcare provider include fever greater than 100.4°F (38°C); change in mental status, such as confusion or lethargy; chills; malodorous urine; and suprapubic or flank pain.

sections.patient_teaching.0.quote: Timed voiding can be used to help a patient regain control of their bladder by urinating on a set schedule (e.g., every hour) whether they feel the urge to urinate or not.

sections.patient_teaching.4.quote: Incontinence underwear has a waterproof liner and built-in cloth pad to absorb large amounts of urine, thereby protecting skin from moisture and controlling odor.
